extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of Stoic philosophy; general readers learning Stoic practice
extracted.subtask_description: A practical guide to Stoic philosophy that explains core Stoic doctrines (physics, logic, ethics) and gives step-by-step practice guidance (Epictetus’s three topics) for correcting judgment, choosing actions, and cultivating gratitude and virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stoic Ontological Theorem (things under our control vs not)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between what is under our control (judgment, impulse, desire, aversion — essentially our prohairesis) and what is not (body, possessions, reputation, public office, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify each thing you encounter as either within your charge or not; focus effort on what is under your charge. Epictetus calls only four things strictly under our control (judgment, impulse, desire, aversion) and adds the use of representations. Misidentifying externals as ours leads to disturbance, lament, reproach, and loss of freedom. Use this distinction continuously to examine opinions and to avoid projecting value onto externals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nothing external is by itself a good or an evil
rubrics_metrics.description: External things (including body and possessions) are indifferent; good and evil are properties of our actions/choices (the outcomes of assent to representations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat wealth, status, or bodily goods as goods in themselves; they are materials for choice. Proper use (guided by wisdom) makes externals profitable; misuse (driven by ignorance) makes them harmful. This underpins Stoic practical goals: avoid seeking externals as ends and avoid repelling them as intrinsic evils.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohairesis (capacity for choice) as locus of moral responsibility and freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: The capacity for choice — prohairesis — is the essential, unhindered aspect of the self and is the proper object of moral cultivation; it cannot be externally compelled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate and purify the prohairesis by inspecting and withholding assent from false judgments. Recognize that, even under external coercion, assent (true acceptance) remains within your power. Moral progress consists in keeping the capacity for choice in good condition, supplied with correct opinions and assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct representations (kataleptic impressions) as the criterion for knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge arises when sensory input (phantasia) is correctly interpreted by the rational soul, producing comprehensive representations (kataleptikai) that correspond to external objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train the intellect to form and recognize comprehensive representations; use logic to test whether a representation corresponds to reality. The ideal sage contains only such correct representations; ordinary humans must constantly examine and correct their beliefs to approach knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of propositional logic and detection of fallacies
rubrics_metrics.description: Stoic logic includes propositional logic (assertibles/axioms and theory of argument/logos) and the study/classification of sophisms; one must learn to recognize valid inference forms and identify fallacies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice testing arguments for validity (e.g., recognize the fallacy 'denying the antecedent'). Logic is essential both for scientific knowledge and everyday discernment; studying sophisms and propositional logic helps prevent assent to deceptive arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epictetus’s tripartite practice order: judgment/desire, action, persuasion
rubrics_metrics.description: Stoic practice follows Epictetus’s three topics, to be studied and practiced in order: (1) judgment or desire (correcting opinions and appetites), (2) action (applying appropriate conduct), (3) persuasion (ensuring and teaching the first two).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin by reforming judgments and impulses (first topic) before moving to appropriate action (second topic). Only those who master the first two should undertake the third (teaching/persuasion). The order is pedagogical and practical: internal revision precedes behavioral change and public persuasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Daily examination and withdrawal of assent from false judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: Regularly re-evaluate representations and consciously withdraw assent from judgments that attribute value to externals or are otherwise false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make this practice habitual: use the Ontological Theorem to scrutinize each judgment, classify what is under your control, and remove assent from false beliefs. Epictetus advises aiming at important internal changes and abandoning some desires entirely rather than moderating them insufficiently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passions as assent to false suppositions; cure by correcting judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Passions (pleasure, suffering, fear, desire) are excessive movements of the soul that arise from assent to false beliefs (e.g., believing externals to be good or evil).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the mental error (false opinion) behind each passion and correct it; the rational counterparts are contentment (for pleasure) and absence of suffering (for suffering). Purifying assent eliminates bad passions and leads to proper, rational responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: The theorem of gratitude: gratitude depends on placing good in what is under our control
rubrics_metrics.description: Gratitude (eucharistia) arises only when one places one's good in things under one's control (the capacity for choice); valuing externals leads to blaming the gods/divinity and impiety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foster piety and gratitude by recognizing Providence and by restricting what you regard as truly good to what depends on your prohairesis. Give thanks for the responsibilities and capacities you genuinely possess rather than for externals you cannot control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three spheres of action implied by the Ontological Theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: The Ontological Theorem implies distinct domains for human action: (1) interiority (thoughts, impulses, assents), (2) physical phenomena (bodies and natural laws), (3) relationships with other humans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the appropriate attitude in each sphere: govern interiority by inspecting assent; understand and work with natural laws for material tasks (e.g., engineering uses of nature); use persuasion and recognize others’ prohaireses in social relations. Do not expect to control spheres that are not yours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue as knowledge; the four cardinal virtues defined epistemically
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtues are excellences (arete/virtus) constituted by knowledge about how to deal with external things. Wisdom (phronesis), temperance (sophrosyne), justice (dikaiosyne), and courage (andreia) are knowledge-based capacities concerning what to do, avoid, assign, and fear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand virtues as cognitive skills: cultivate the knowledge component that tells you what is necessary, what to seek or avoid, what belongs to whom, and what should be feared. Because virtue is knowledge, it alone suffices for happiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental Stoic ethical theorem: wisdom alone is good; ignorance alone is bad
rubrics_metrics.description: Only wisdom counts as a genuine good; only ignorance counts as a genuine bad; externals are indifferent and matter only insofar as wisdom uses them well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Orient moral education toward acquiring knowledge/wisdom rather than pursuing externals. Recognize that with wisdom, external disadvantages (e.g., poverty) are bearable; without wisdom, externals become destructive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four human roles to identify for proper action and vocational choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Panaetius’s four roles: (1) rational animal (moral character arising from rationality), (2) individual particular character (physical/psychic qualities), (3) circumstances (fortune into which one is born), (4) profession (chosen).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To fulfill roles well: understand human nature and your moral capacities (role 1); know your individual strengths/limits to choose suitable tasks (role 2); be aware of social circumstances and adapt (role 3); freely choose a profession aligned with your qualities (role 4). Self-knowledge ensures appropriate vocational decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stoic conception of Providence and the imperfect-but-harmonious cosmos
rubrics_metrics.description: Providence is the cosmic order (Nature/pneuma) that is overall beautiful and governing, but not perfect in the modern sense; matter resists pneumatic activity and Divinity cannot foresee all causal interactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept that Providence manifests in generic, universal harmony rather than perfect outcomes for individuals; expect imperfections (disease, unintended side effects). Use this understanding to moderate expectations and to focus on what one can do within one’s sphere of responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human as exegete: ultimate end is interpretation through knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Epictetus frames the human telos as that of an exegete — an interpreter of the Cosmos — because virtue is knowledge and realization consists in understanding the world and oneself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pursue knowledge through philosophical/scientific dialogue and spiritual practice; interpret events and your role in the cosmic order as a way to realize rational nature and fulfill responsibility to assist Nature where appropriate.
